conflicts.meeting_title: Joint City County Committee Meeting Oct. 10, 2023
conflicts.issue: Mid-Year Supplemental Funding Priorities (Museum of Durham History vs. Employee Pay and Emergency Shelter)
conflicts.summary: Committee members expressed differing views on whether to entertain a mid-year supplemental funding request for the Museum of Durham History given competing urgent needs for city employee pay and emergency domestic violence shelter funding.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question mid-year museum funding when employee compensation and emergency DV shelter needs remain strained.
side_a_arguments: The city faces ongoing challenges paying its workforce and just heard an urgent $250,000 request for a 24-hour domestic violence shelter.
Mid-year requests outside the adopted FY23-24 budget cycle are difficult to accommodate.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support investing in the Museum of Durham History to leverage private philanthropy and grow tourism tax revenue.
side_b_arguments: Durham's current museum facilities are inadequate, and public investment is needed to overcome private donor fatigue.
Cultural and tourism investments generate sales and occupancy taxes that help pay for core services and crisis response.
conflicts.resolution: No committee vote was taken on funding; members agreed to inform full City Council and County Commissioners of both supplemental requests.

meetings.title: Joint City County Committee Meeting Oct. 10, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The Joint City-County Committee heard presentations from Durham Department of Social Services (DSS) leadership on looming rental assistance gaps as federal emergency rental funds expire, as well as proposed enhancements to the joint Low-Income Homeowner Relief tax subsidy program for seniors 60 and older below 30% AMI. Committee members also heard a $250,000 emergency funding request to sustain Durham's 24-hour domestic violence and sexual assault shelter following state pass-through cuts, and a supplemental funding request for the Museum of Durham History expansion study and development position. While members debated balancing mid-year cultural investments against employee pay pressures and emergency shelter needs, the committee agreed to relay both funding requests to their respective full boards and unanimously approved the 2024 Joint City-County Committee meeting schedule.

agenda_items.title: DSS Emergency Rental Assistance and Eviction Diversion Post-Federal Funding
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DSS Director Maggie Cveticanin and staff reported that federal ERAP dollars are nearly depleted while applicants average five or more months behind on rent ($5,402 average assistance) and over half of Durham renters pay over 30% of income toward rent. Officials urged holistic multi-agency coordination across housing, transit, and childcare rather than short-term landlord payments alone.

agenda_items.title: Low-Income Homeowner Relief Property Tax Subsidy Program Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DSS presented outcomes from the joint city-county property tax subsidy program (339 viable applications, 200 approved at an average of $714 per household) and proposed paying full tax bills for seniors 60+ below 30% AMI. Staff noted targeted outreach in zip codes 27704 and 27707, including Braggtown, East Durham, Wellons Village, and Lakewood.

agenda_items.title: Emergency Domestic Violence / Sexual Assault Shelter Supplemental Funding Ask
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Representatives requested $250,000 in bridge funding and ongoing city/county line-item support for Durham's sole 24-hour emergency domestic violence and sexual assault shelter after losing state-funneled federal funds. Committee members expressed strong sympathy and support for bringing the request back to both governing bodies.

agenda_items.title: Museum of Durham History Expansion Study and Staffing Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Museum leaders presented a supplemental budget request for a revised program study, site test-fit analysis, and a full-time development staff position, citing private donor fatigue and potential occupancy/sales tax returns. Committee members questioned taking on mid-year supplemental asks amid city employee compensation challenges and domestic violence shelter needs, agreeing to forward both asks to full Council and the County Board.

agenda_items.title: Committee Procedural Motion and 2024 Joint City-County Meeting Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The committee approved an unspecified procedural motion followed by the 2024 Joint City-County Committee meeting schedule (Feb. 13, Apr. 9, Jun. 11, Aug. 13, Oct. 8, and Dec. 10, 2024). Members noted it was the final joint committee meeting under Mayor Elaine O'Neal's term.

meetings.title: Special Joint City Council & Board of County Commissioners Comprehensive Plan Public Hearing
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Mayor Elaine O'Neal co-presided over the August 31, 2023 Special Joint City Council and Board of County Commissioners Public Hearing to take community testimony on the draft Durham Comprehensive Plan ahead of formal October adoption votes. City-County Planning Department staff (Lisa Miller and Sara Young) outlined the growth management strategy, proposed reducing the existing 2005 Suburban Tier by approximately 10.8 square miles to establish the Urban Growth Boundary (UGB) while accommodating a projected 143,000 additional housing units, and introduced edits to Policies 164 and 165 along with six contested fringe areas. Roughly sixty-five in-person and remote speakers debated keeping Arrowhead, Patterson Road, Cheek/Redwood Road, and Farrington Mill Road inside versus outside the UGB and Southeast Future Growth Area, weighing affordable housing supply and landowner equity against watershed protection, septic/infrastructure capacity, and rural preservation; no board votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Joint Public Hearing Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the joint meeting and conducted roll calls confirming all five County Commissioners (Howerton, Jacobs, Burns, Allam, Carter) and City Council members were present. Chair Howerton read the public charge and confirmed that over 50 in-person speakers and 15+ virtual speakers had registered, clarifying that elected officials would listen without back-and-forth debate and deliberate separately in subsequent meetings.

agenda_items.title: Staff Presentation: Draft Durham Comprehensive Plan, UGB Reduction, and Policies 164-165
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City-County Planning Assistant Director Lisa Miller and Director Sara Young summarized the three-year Comprehensive Plan process, emphasizing smart infill growth, housing supply estimates (143,000 potential units versus 60,000 needed by 2050), and the proposed 10.8-square-mile reduction from the 2005 Suburban Tier to form the Urban Growth Boundary. Staff highlighted Planning Commission-recommended edits to Policy 165 requiring case-by-case map amendments to demonstrate affordable housing, environmental, and equity benefits, and Policy 164 mandating biennial UGB assessments. Staff also reviewed six disputed areas—Stagville/Old Oxford, Farrington Mill, Patterson Road, Cheek/Redwood, Hamlin Road, and the northwest corner of the Southeast Future Growth Area.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Testimony on Comprehensive Plan, Urban Growth Boundary, and Rural Preservation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Across nearly three hours of in-person and remote testimony, Arrowhead landowner Adam Abram, attorney Patrick Byker, homebuilders representatives (John Hasbrouck, Holly Fraccaro), engineers (Tim Sivers), and landowners on Patterson, Cheek, and Farrington Mill Roads urged retaining existing Suburban Tier parcels in the UGB to support housing affordability, prevent low-density two-acre sprawl, and protect property values. Conversely, numerous Arrowhead and Southeast Durham residents, Care for Durham conservation advocates, coalition speakers (Coalition for Affordable Housing and Transit), and environmental voices cited Policy 166 watershed rules, Voluntary Agricultural District pledges, Forest View Elementary overcrowding (104% capacity), Lick Creek stormwater degradation, and transit/infrastructure costs in supporting the staff/Planning Commission map keeping Arrowhead and rural fringe tracts outside the UGB. Chair Howerton closed the public hearing at 03:13:42 without board action.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Public hearing closed for future board deliberation)

meetings.title: Joint City-County Committee Meeting June 13, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The June 13, 2023 Joint City-County Committee meeting proceeded without a City Council quorum, so no formal votes were taken on absences or minutes. Senior Planner Carl Kolosna briefed elected officials on the draft 2023 Durham Comprehensive Plan and six disputed Urban Growth Boundary and Future Growth Area map revisions ahead of the August 31 public hearing, while Southeast Durham residents raised urgent concerns over mass grading, Lick Creek sedimentation, and rural outreach. The committee also received an emotional report on the May 6 Youth Community Hackathon to Prevent Gun Violence (highlighting mental-health needs and a $2,000 pay shortfall for student consultants), an overview of American Red Cross disaster preparedness partnerships, and a 10th-anniversary expansion and funding update from the Museum of Durham History.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Update and UGB/FGA Discussion Points
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Carl Kolosna presented the draft 2023 Comprehensive Plan and six map areas where property owners sought re-inclusion in the Urban Growth Boundary or staff proposed Future Growth Area revisions. Residents Rebecca Freeman, Thomas Freeman, Pam Williams, and Lana Ball urged holding the UGB line and halting mass grading around Kemp Road, NC 98, and Lick Creek to protect Falls Lake, prompting Mayor O'Neal to urge colleagues to tour affected Southeast Durham sites.

agenda_items.title: Youth Community Hackathon to Prevent Gun Violence & Prescriptions for Repair Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Co-chairs Marcia Owen and Xavier Cason and organizer Kelly presented outcomes from the May 6 Youth Community Hackathon (20 DPS students calling for trusted adults trained in mental health, school wellness days, and gun-safety laws). Officials and City Manager Wanda Page addressed a $2,000 discrepancy after students were advertised $25/hour but funded at $25/day ($6,000 city allocation out of $13,475 requested), agreeing to seek a city/county remedy and clarify task-force funding protocols.

agenda_items.title: American Red Cross Central NC Chapter Preparedness and Partnership Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Executive Director Lori Hughes and Disaster Program Specialist Sweetly Sanders outlined Red Cross services in Durham—including over $240,000 in disaster aid since 2022, Sound the Alarm free smoke alarms, youth preparedness, shelter training with DPS nurses, and hands-only CPR—and discussed expanding partnerships with DHA, Durham Tech, and city/county emergency management.

agenda_items.title: Museum of Durham History 10th-Anniversary and Facility Expansion Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Executive Director Patrick Mucklow presented the museum's 10th-anniversary update, requesting $568,000 for 505 W. Chapel Hill St expansion design and $108,000 in immediate operating/staffing support (including a 10% staff raise and $20/hour weekend pay). Officials noted NCGS 14-234.3 conflict-of-interest rules prevent nonprofit board members from chairing joint review committees and referred the $108,000 request to the city and county managers ahead of an August 8 follow-up.

meetings.title: Durham City-County Joint Meeting for April 11, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Durham County Commissioners and City of Durham leaders convened for the April 11, 2023 Joint City-County Meeting, with Commissioner Wendy Jacobs joining virtually while traveling. Durham Crisis Response Center Executive Director Damien Talley provided a pre-opening update on the Family Justice Center (set to open April 24, 2023) and its Spanish-language and immigrant victim services. Leaders also strategized on convening a rapid community 'roll call' of nonprofits to coordinate summer youth camp capacity and promote an April 22 joint job fair, and the Mayor presented four shovel-ready affordable housing developments seeking County matching gap funds alongside $10 million committed by the City.

agenda_items.title: Introductions and Family Justice Center / Durham Crisis Response Center Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page, City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg, Commissioner Nida Allam, Durham Crisis Response Center Executive Director Damien Talley, and County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell opened with introductions, noting Commissioner Wendy Jacobs participated via Zoom while traveling. Talley updated officials on the Family Justice Center's April 24, 2023 grand opening, highlighting Legal Aid and Sheriff's Office co-location, 15 Latinx women and children sheltered via the Spanish crisis line, and 165 individuals served by immigrant services.

agenda_items.title: Summer Youth Programming Roll Call of Nonprofits and Joint Job Fair
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Officials discussed addressing summer programming gaps for older youth beyond the roughly 5,000 younger students reached by Durham Public Schools summer programs. Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Mayor/board colleagues supported convening a rapid 'roll call' of local nonprofits (such as Durham Children's Initiative, YMCA, Museum of Life and Science, Boys & Girls Club, and Salvation Army) to inventory camp seats, scholarships, and donated resources without duplicating existing fundraising, alongside a joint City-County-DPS job fair on April 22.

agenda_items.title: Item #4: Affordable Housing Partnerships — Four Shovel-Ready City RFP Priority Projects
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Mayor outlined four shovel-ready affordable housing developments from the City's RFP round that lacked full gap financing—noting the City allocated $10 million and hoped the County would match each project (each needing just under $5 million from the City): East Geer Street (~84 units at 30%–80% AMI), the Durham Tech Briggs Avenue initiative (120+ units prioritizing DTCC students), Dearborn Drive Multifamily (~200 units with 100 at 60% AMI plus permanent space for the VFW), and Sandy Ridge Phase 2. Leaders thanked City and County housing staff (Bertha and Claudia) and noted the next joint meeting would be June 13.
